thread_tweets.text:
Base head Jesse Pollak says teams of AI agents on open models could outpace frontier models: the market for them will emerge onchain

"I think one of our guiding beliefs is that we think that agents are going to be the majority of actors in the new global economy over the next few years."

"We're almost to the point where instead of calling Base the blockchain for global finance, we want to say the blockchain for agent finance, because we think that so much of the way that money moves is going to start to be driven by agents."

"Today we have this almost monopoly where the easiest way to get really powerful work done is to use a frontier model."

"Our thesis is actually that we're going to increasingly see agents built on open models that work in teams, where agents are collaborating and you can actually farm out a piece of work and then it can be multiplexed across many agents."

"In the same way that a team of people can often outpace the smartest individual, a team of agents may be able to outpace the smartest agent."

"Naturally the place where that market's going to emerge is going to be onchain, because agents naturally gravitate towards programmable money because they are programmable themselves."

I don’t know a single investor who feels misled. And I know almost all of the large ones personally.

Jensen consistently said beginning in mid/late 2025 that “we are assuming/forecasting China datacenter sales to be zero” and then on the calls Colette would note that approved China datacenter sales were sub 1% of revenue. No one cares abt that differential (forecasting zero vs. sub 1%). Most recent disclosure of $2.4b was more precise but directionally consistent at 2% of quarterly revenue. Also gaming and workstation GPUs are not datacenter GPUs.

And investors understood that SE Asian, European and US clouds/hyperscalers were renting GPUs to Chinese labs from all of those geographies (ie American hyperscalers were renting GPUs to Chinese labs from their SE Asian, European and American availability zones). Which is obviously the most pro-national security policy of all as can literally turn them off in any conflict. This would dramatically curtail China’s ability to use AI (need inference capacity) overnight. This gave America arguably more leverage over China than they had over us through rare earths. And our leverage would have grown every year while theirs shrank.

Now Alibaba is saying that Huawei will be at parity (tho way less power efficient but China has loads of power) in a year. Those Huawei systems will undoubtedly make their way to Russia, North Korea and Iran and endanger America due to well-intentioned China Hawks in DC and the media.

Our old policy guaranteed America would always be ahead. New course much riskier imo.

My weekend thoughts on #uranium, #silver, #gold and HydroGraph $HGRAF

Uranium stocks have been hammered. Uranium itself is still around $90/lb. I expect a much higher uranium price in 2027, and I’m still waiting another month or two before adding heavily to the miners. Here’s why.

Uranium

When uranium juniors sell off across the board, I look at how much drilling each one can fund with the cash it already has. The drill program costs just as much after a sell-off. If the share price halves, an explorer has to issue twice as many shares to raise the same money. And that assumes investors are willing to write the cheque.

Producers have their own problem. Miss a production target and you may have to buy uranium on the spot market to deliver into a contract you signed years ago at a lower price. Meanwhile, the cost of labour, materials and construction has gone up. How sad is that? You are a producer, the LT price is ok, but you keep losing money because of past mistakes.

Look at what the big producers actually got paid in Q3. Spot averaged US$88.56/lb. Kazatomprom’s group realized US$81.50. Cameco realized US$65.78. That’s nearly US$23 below spot for Cameco. My view is that producers locked in too many pounds too cheaply. Utilities will have to offer better terms if they want someone to build the next generation of mines.

And does $90/lb really sound expensive? Uranium hit $136 in 2007. That was nearly 20 years of inflation ago. At today’s construction costs, plenty of greenfield projects still struggle to offer a return worth the risk. Even at $150/lb, I’d question how quickly the industry could deliver enough uranium. A utility can raise its bid tomorrow. A miner still needs years to permit, finance and build.

I expect larger producers to pick up some of the better juniors. Others could face another round of selling if their market caps fall far enough to get them dropped from an index. I’m looking for cash in the bank, a manageable burn rate and projects whose economics hold up at today’s costs. For investors who want exposure to physical uranium, there’s #SPUT. For a basket of miners, there are uranium equity ETFs.

One more thing to remember when the tide turns. If the juniors double or triple, expect a wave of financings. A CEO who struggled to raise money at the bottom will take that call at twice the price.

Gold, silver and the signal I’m watching

With uranium, I can look at what utilities need and what the mines can deliver. Gold and silver are harder to call. Investment flows can turn quickly, and silver has industrial demand in the mix as well.

Right now, I’m watching oil. A sustained drop should feed through to lower headline inflation over the coming months. If markets start pricing in rate cuts and real yields roll over, I expect gold and silver to turn well before the first cut. Easier financing would give uranium equities room to run, too. Until then, I see more downside in precious metals.

Why HydroGraph is my largest holding

How do you sell serious tonnage of a material that works at a dose of just 200 grams? Look at what those 200 grams go into.

In a peer-reviewed study published in October, Arizona State researchers used 200 grams of HydroGraph graphene per tonne of binder in 3D-printed mortar. They measured gains of up to 25% in compressive and flexural strength. At that dose, every million tonnes of binder treated would use 200 tonnes of graphene. That’s why the size of the end market matters so much to me.

The plastics results are just as striking. In HydroGraph’s epoxy tests, replacing a small amount of carbon black with 0.04% graphene cut electrical resistivity to one-110th of its original value. The total amount of conductive filler stayed the same.

My favourite example comes from DB Chem. It needed an antistatic plastic film, but even at 30% carbon black, the affordable grade couldn’t meet the target. With 15% carbon black and just 0.2% HydroGraph graphene, the film hit the target, was easier to form and cost about the same to formulate. That’s a result a purchasing manager can act on.

Then there’s Sparc Technologies. After 16 weeks of corrosion testing, rust had spread 25% less from a scratch in a commercial epoxy coating containing Sparc’s HydroGraph-based additive. Sparc says a successful 4,200-hour test would take the companies into negotiations for a supply agreement. That’s one potential customer with a specific result and a clear next decision.

CEO Kjirstin Breure’s two November interviews with Jay Taylor are worth putting together. On November 5, she explained how the graphene paste makes it easier for manufacturers to use the material. More than 30 customers have already received samples. In the November 19 follow-up, she discussed patents for specific applications, including conductive plastics, and said a manufacturer was already lined up to build more Hyperion reactors.

Several customers have moved on to negotiating prices, volumes and supply terms. And look at who HydroGraph hired this week to close those deals. New chief commercial officer Hector Miravete previously led commercial strategy for a Johnson Matthey catalyst portfolio generating more than $700 million in annual revenue. He knows what it takes to sell a specialized material to industrial buyers year after year.

Now put the capital requirements alongside the mining economics above. HydroGraph raised C$70.4 million. What does it cost to get Bellville up and running? Roughly US$8 million for the building and its first six reactors, according to CEO Kjirstin Breure. That gives HydroGraph about 60 tons of annual capacity at Bellville, with room to scale to 360 as orders come in.

I expect hockey-stick revenue growth to begin in 2027, and I see a credible path to break-even that year without another equity raise. The milestone I’m watching most closely is the first repeat order with meaningful volume. That’s when we start to learn what one qualified application is worth to HydroGraph every year. Then run the same exercise across plastics, coatings, cement and rubber. That’s why $HGRAF is my number one investment.

Just my weekend thoughts. As always, do your own DD.

Some random, unfiltered thoughts on AI and the market:

The gulf between “San Francisco” and “New York” has never been wider than it is right now 

AI is accelerating in capability, rapidly and in a way that is structurally changing, and in many ways upending, the nature of the firm and the fundamentals of capitalism

If that sounds extreme, consider that Anthropic has ~6,000 employees, Meta has 67,000, and both companies are worth ~$1.5T

Talk to your average startup and it’s clear that, given the opportunity to start from scratch, nobody is building their companies “the old way.” 

Talk to your average Fortune 500 company and it’s clear that getting an AI agent into production at scale is a Herculean task

Intelligence may not be the bottleneck, but firms built from the foundational assumption that intelligence is improving quickly in capability and price are scaling at a genuinely unbelievably velocity

There’s a reason Zuck wanted to fire 60% of many of the teams at his company, in large part likely out of frustration that he can’t start from scratch like his competitors had the luxury of doing

A structurally weaker Nvidia and OpenAI have minimal impact on the pace and impact of AI diffusing across the economy (“San Francisco”), but completely breaks the models built in “New York.” Hence the absolute freak-out these last few weeks. It was all priced to go perfectly and now things are not perfect 

But for the boots on the ground, AI will not slow down. And counterintuitively, economic weakness might accelerate diffusion. After all, tokens are much more fungible and flexible than people

Where does that leave us? I think firmly in the second phase of the AI build-out. Real value is being built in the app layer (though how defensible it is…TBD).  

Trying to predict the next bottleneck, or whether Washington does this or that other thing wrt policy, or exactly how many data centers get built out…who can say? Certainly not me. It’s not the bet I’m trying to make 

I’m looking at who wins from rapidly improving intelligence available at increasingly cheaper prices, and critically, which leaders are able to move with conviction into this new operating paradigm

5: where's the first trouble overhead?
old support becomes resistance. for this bounce that's $62,000-$66,000.

what would change my mind: daily and weekly closes below $58,625, or a daily close back above $62,000-$66,000.

save this for the future broski’s!

Flashback to June 14, 2024.

At the time, frontier AI models have zero fluid intelligence. They score around 5% on ARC 1. They can't reliably add two numbers. They make laughable logic errors every other prompt. Reasoning models don't exist. Coding agents don't exist. Claude Code doesn't exist. "Code gen" is a complete joke. Scaling up next-token prediction based on web text data is hitting a wall.

What if a time traveler told you that, by November 2026...

• AI models would have human-like fluid intelligence, thanks to a new paradigm: test-time induction (modern reasoning models).
• Not only would ARC 1 be saturated, but unreleased benchmarks 10x harder (ARC 2) and 100x harder (ARC 3) would be saturated too.
• Nearly all code would be written by AI, and models could one-shot complex codebases flawlessly.
• AI models would be solving multiple Millennium Prize problems.
• OpenAI's valuation would be 15x higher, and Anthropic's would be 85x higher.

And on top of all that...

• Nvidia would still hold ~80% of the AI compute market.
• Nvidia would have grown its revenue and earnings 4.5x.
• Nvidia would still be growing 75% a year.
• Nvidia would have even higher operating margins (67% vs. 65% back then).

Based on that information, straight from the future, would you have bought NVDA?

If you answered yes -- congrats. Today, 2.5 years later, you'd be down 5% on your investment (even more after inflation).

𝗪𝗘𝗘𝗞𝗘𝗡𝗗 𝗠𝗨𝗦𝗜𝗡𝗚𝗦: 𝗟𝗘𝗦𝗦𝗢𝗡𝗦 𝗙𝗥𝗢𝗠 𝗔 𝗕𝗥𝗨𝗧𝗔𝗟 𝗪𝗘𝗘𝗞

A good time for reflection, for myself and anyone using different strategies to navigate the markets. What worked, what didn’t, and what can we learn?

𝗟𝗘𝗦𝗦𝗢𝗡 𝟭: 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗩𝗜𝗫 𝗛𝗔𝗦 𝗕𝗘𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗘 𝗣𝗥𝗔𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗖𝗔𝗟𝗟𝗬 𝗨𝗡𝗨𝗦𝗔𝗕𝗟𝗘

One of my favorite indicators has lost much of its value. A sudden 10% drop in the VIX after a market decline used to signal improving sentiment. Now it drops 10%, jumps 15% the next day, and falls another 15%.

The signal has become noise. At least for now, I’m taking it off the table.

Just because something worked for years doesn’t mean it will continue working. When reality proves otherwise, abandon it.

𝗟𝗘𝗦𝗦𝗢𝗡 𝟮: MOST 𝗧𝗘𝗖𝗛𝗡𝗜𝗖𝗔𝗟 𝗔𝗡𝗔𝗟𝗬𝗦𝗜𝗦 𝗜𝗦 𝗪𝗢𝗥𝗧𝗛𝗟𝗘𝗦𝗦

Bitcoin is the perfect example. $68K is critical support. Once broken, $65K becomes critical. Then $62K. Then $58K.

Eventually Bitcoin bounces somewhere, and technicians proudly announce that it bounced off support.

A system that explains everything after it happens but tells you nothing useful beforehand has zero value.

𝗟𝗘𝗦𝗦𝗢𝗡 𝟯: 𝗔𝗩𝗢𝗜𝗗 𝗦𝗣𝗘𝗖𝗨𝗟𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗩𝗘 𝗚𝗥𝗢𝗪𝗧𝗛 𝗦𝗧𝗢𝗖𝗞𝗦

Look at $IREN, $NBIS, $OKLO, $RGTI, $CRWV, $CIFR, $APLD and others. Many have suffered enormous drawdowns, some approaching 70% to 80%.

These stocks are often lottery tickets purchased at the worst possible time.

By the time everyone discovers the next revolutionary company, the price already reflects a dream that may never materialize.

A few might succeed, but many won’t. Even successful businesses can become terrible investments when purchased at hype valuations.

𝗟𝗘𝗦𝗦𝗢𝗡 𝟰: 𝗧𝗔𝗞𝗘 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗙𝗜𝗧𝗦 𝗔𝗡𝗗 𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗬 𝗛𝗨𝗠𝗕𝗟𝗘

If your portfolio is up 50% or 100% in a year, congratulations. But don’t confuse extraordinary returns with your normal earning power.

We’ve seen hedge funds up 30% or 40% give back everything and turn negative.

I learned this lesson myself this quarter.

Take profits, reduce risk, and protect what you’ve earned. There’s nothing wrong with leaving money on the table.

𝗟𝗘𝗦𝗦𝗢𝗡 𝟱: 𝗡𝗘𝗩𝗘𝗥 𝗙𝗔𝗟𝗟 𝗜𝗡 𝗟𝗢𝗩𝗘 𝗪𝗜𝗧𝗛 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗦𝗧𝗢𝗥𝗬

Stocks can rise 100% or 300% simply because investors fall in love with a dream.

Very few dreams become reality. Identifying the winners consistently is extremely difficult. I doubt even I could do it.

The smart approach is to buy before the hype and sell when everyone else falls in love with the story.

Being right about a company isn’t the same as making money from its stock.

𝗟𝗘𝗦𝗦𝗢𝗡 𝟲: 𝗡𝗢𝗧𝗛𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗜𝗦 𝗜𝗠𝗠𝗨𝗡𝗘 𝗧𝗢 𝗥𝗜𝗦𝗞

If $NVDA, the golden poster child of corporate excellence, can lose 45% in such a short period, while even allegations of fraud enter the conversation, what company is truly immune?

Extraordinary earnings, technology and market dominance don’t protect shareholders when sentiment changes.

Which raises the most interesting question of the week: What exactly is the market so afraid of?

𝗟𝗘𝗦𝗦𝗢𝗡 𝟳: 𝗪𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗗𝗜𝗗 𝗪𝗢𝗥𝗞? $VIX 𝗕𝗔𝗖𝗞𝗪𝗔𝗥𝗗𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡

One signal that continues to deserve respect. When the VIX term structure moves into significant backwardation, avoid adding risk.

Tom Lee called it a buying opportunity. The market subsequently fell another 8%.

Don’t be angry with Tom Lee or Michael Saylor. They’re promoters. The mistake is believing their predictions have special value.

Tom Lee reportedly earns around $20 million a year telling people stocks will eventually go up.

That’s like paying someone $20 million to stand outside in January and announce that summer is coming.

Eventually, he’ll be right.

𝗙𝗜𝗡𝗔𝗟 𝗧𝗛𝗢𝗨𝗚𝗛𝗧

The purpose of reflection isn’t to defend our decisions. It’s to recognize what stopped working, where we became overconfident, and what needs to change.

Stay humble. Stay flexible. Protect your capital.

Have a great weekend.

David Friedberg: Why the AI Job Loss Narrative is Bullsh*t

“The job loss narrative is bullsh*t. It's also why ‘Everyone is going to end up on welfare,’ is bullsh*t. (And) ‘We need the government to step in and provide UBI,’ is bullsh*t.

Because with any other kind of frontier moment in human history, it's the new jobs, the new industries get created before the old ones are irrelevant.

I think the biggest opportunity for AI is on the frontier. That is where basically businesses and people can do things that humans and businesses have never been able to do before.

And that means crafting solutions to really difficult engineering problems, to really difficult scientific problems, to previously intractable problems.

And that's where I think that the frontier gets expanded by 100x or 1,000x versus AI being some iteration on existing business processes to save money and make things more efficient, which is where people natively go because most people don't work on the frontier, and they're not pushing the envelope on what's possible.

So their mind is always about, ‘Well, how does this change my job?’ And then you immediately get fearful about your job getting recast.

And the truth is, that's not the typical use case. The typical use case where we spend time and spend tokens is doing things that we've never done before, figuring out how to solve those really tough problems, how to do it quickly, how to do it efficiently, and that means humans generally can expand our frontiers, our horizons.”

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
I genuinely agree with this take, and don't know why there's so much conflict about it. As much as BTC still drives altcoin movements today, it is quite clear that the trend is weakening and will continue to weaken. And that is a good thing. Hyperliquid & Venice both up >100% YTD within a muted BTC environment.

What we all want is a bifurcation of the market where digital-equity-esque assets are unencumbered by digital SoV price movements. The truth is it, that as the industry continues to print out once-a-year generational companies that are high-growth, make recurring money, and decide to launch a token, that these BUSINESSES should not have their fundamental performance tied to the price of a digital rock which trades based solely on flows and not on fundamentals

A better example would be if the price-action of equities was wholly dependent on how Gold traded. These two assets should move *independently* of each other. Of course, they are usually linked by macro-economic conditions - e.g Gold going up = economic uncertainty so flight to store of value = usually means equities are not doing too hot

But it's more pointing to a simpler fact that Gold should not determine (emphasis on determine here) how equities trade, i.e it's not a cause and effect relationship

However, for most digital assets, Bitcoin is a direct cause and effect relationship across the broader backdrop of the market. And that has made sense considering that for the past 5+ years, Bitcoin was seen as a risk-asset alongside the broader crypo-economic class as well. Bitcoin was touted as a store of value, but in reality, was really just an altcoin, and then altcoins were extremely high beta bitcoins.

However, the relationship now should and has begun to change, because Bitcoin is no longer being treated in the same vein as altcoins. Yes, it is still very much a risk assets in some regimes. But it in many ways has become institutionalized, and that usually leads to lower volatility (-50% drawdown from the 2025 top rather than a -80% drawdown from the 2021 top);  and conversely, you can also imagine that there will be lesser upside volatility as well.

Trad institutions I talk to see Bitcoin as this unironic gold-alternative-with-high-beta-and-asymmetric-upside that they only buy if they think Gold is going to go up, or if it gets cheap enough, or if they think the crypto market has some reason to do well.

Whereas, digital-assets like Hyperliquid, have way more going for it than that. And so, it is natural to want and even to bet on this de-correlating relationship. After all, if Hyperliquid manages to onbaord traditional equities, and their usage doubles, why should the price action of Bitcoin matter? All that matters for Hyperliquid is how the underlying business performs - Bitcoin going up is just an added tailwind, not the necessary ingredient.

And then you extend this logic to the handful of crypto-token-businesses that exist today, and you basically arrive at Jeff's take! I would like to bet on more good crypto-businesses with a token because their business is good, not because I believe Bitcoin can go up.

Over the past couple weeks we've met with management teams across memory, optics, neoclouds, semis, semi cap equipment and substrates.

Everyone is frustrated and confused about their stock prices but everyone is still very, very bullish.

Everyone expects 2027 capex to be significantly higher than 2026 and they expect 2028 capex to be moderately to significantly higher than 2027. 

Everyone knows the YoY capex growth rates will decelerate but the total dollars spent will continue to get bigger... at least for the next few years. Everyone says we're still in the early innings of ai adoption. 

Every company in the ai ecosystem is 50-100% sold out for 2027 and 40-80% sold out for 2028. 

Everyone is sitting on LTAs from the hyperscalers... some of those LTAs are getting signed and they last anywhere from 3 years to 6+ years... and they're getting done at record prices and record margins. Customers can't take the chance of not having enough supply to meet their needs over the next 3-5 years... locking up supply at record prices is better than not having enough supply when it's needed the most. 

Some of these LTAs could consume more than 50% of their supply over the next 2-3 years and at least one company has an LTA that would consume 75% of their capacity over the next 2-3 years. 

Neoclouds continue to see demand that is 5-10x higher than capacity. Many of them are saying the financing concerns are overblown. They're seeing 3-5 year deals get signed at 10-20% higher prices that the first half of 2026 and they think deals signed in the first half of 2027 will have 10-20% higher prices than deals signed in the second half of 2026. Power is still a big bottleneck and many sites are dealing with small construction delays but nothing is getting canceled. Customers are desperate for compute. Many of the neoclouds are trying to reserve 10-15% of capacity for shorter term deals and spot market because rates are 2-3x higher than the 3-5 year deals. 

Memory companies say demand will outstrip supply until 2029 at the earliest. They are very confident LTAs won't get cancelled because even at record prices for memory, the customers have enough margin to make it work. 

I know there's lots of fear and uncertainty in the market right now but it's not showing up in the demand... it remains stronger than ever... many backlogs are growing faster than current revenues.

In 20+ years of investing, I've honestly never seen this much dislocation between fundamentals and valuations. This is truly a historic time to be an investor and not in a good way. It's very hard to be patient and lean into your conviction/thesis during times like this but that's probably the right strategy for most long-term investors.

You can learn a lot about the next AI breakthrough by just reading AI labs and RL env startups’ job posts.

I’ve been looking at OpenAI, Anthropic, Mercor etc… and cross-referencing what they’re hiring for with benchmarks models still struggle on. A few things stand out.

Anthropic has a computational chemistry role explicitly about building RL environments to teach Claude reaction prediction, synthesis planning, etc. They also want an antibody scientist to test AI-designed candidates and feed the experimental results back to researchers. Pretty concrete.

On OpenAI’s job board, the Science data role says their current focus is biology and chemistry. Both labs are also hiring people to build RL environments for chip design: generate hardware descriptions, verify them, optimize power and performance…

On Mercor, investment banking and private equity projects advertise $130–180/hour. They want experts to build financial tasks and review model outputs. Meanwhile, the leading full-task score on MBABench 2.0 is only 15.8%. Lots of room to improve there.

Same pattern in healthcare: Mercor recruits specialist physicians, OpenAI explicitly hires for health RL environments, and the published DAYJOB Healthcare evaluation tops out around 25%.

Obviously a job posting doesn’t guarantee a breakthrough. But when expert hiring, training environments and unsaturated benchmarks all point to the same work… that’s worth paying attention to.

My bets: healthcare, financial workflows, chemistry, computational biology and chip design.
